original_interpretation: In July 2024 TSMC's chairman said AI accelerator and CoWoS supply could not reach balance with demand, that supply would stay very tight probably through 2025, and that he hoped it would ease in 2026.
evidence_found: C.C. Wei: "Gokul, I also tried to reach the supply and demand balance, but I cannot today. The demand is so high. I had to work very hard to meet my customers' demand. We continue to increase. I hope, sometime in 2025 or 2026, I could reach the balance." ... "The supply continue to be very tight, all the way to probably 2025, and I hope it can be eased in 2026." (TSMC 2Q24 transcript (Refinitiv edited transcript, 18 July 2024), Q&A, answer to Gokul Hariharan, JPMorgan). Question asked about "supply, demand balance for AI accelerator and CoWoS advanced packaging capacity".
notes: PDF re-downloaded and text extracted locally (WebFetch's own summary of this PDF invented quotes; the extracted text matches the researcher's quotes). Wei is listed as Chairman & CEO. reported_claim / investor_presentation classification is correct.

original_interpretation: TSMC said in July 2024 that its CoWoS capacity more than doubled from 2023 to 2024 and that it aimed to double or more than double it again in 2025, while also working with OSAT partners.
evidence_found: C.C. Wei: "When I say that we doubled the capacity, this is the summing all the different version of the CoWoS together." ... "So from last year to this year, we have more than doubled. And as I said, from this year to next year, we want to double again or, probably, we want to more than double again. But still, I have to work with our OSAT partner to increase the overall supply to support my customer." (TSMC 2Q24 transcript (Refinitiv edited transcript, 18 July 2024), Q&A, answer to Charles Shi)
notes: Capacity doubling is across all CoWoS variants summed, per Wei. Management statement, correctly a reported_claim.

original_interpretation: The CoWoS/AI-silicon bottleneck has lasted from 2023 into at least 2026: TSMC's expected date for supply-demand balance slipped from end-2024 (as recalled by an analyst in July 2024) to '2025 or 2026' (July 2024) and then to working to 'narrow the gap' through 2026-2027 (January 2026).
evidence_found: 2Q24: analyst Gokul Hariharan: "C.C., you mentioned we expect to see supply ... demand to reach balance by end of this year"; Wei: "I hope, sometime in 2025 or 2026, I could reach the balance." 4Q24 (16 Jan 2025): "today is all AI focused, and we have very tight capacity and cannot even meet customers' need." 4Q25 (15 Jan 2026): "The capacity is very tight. We work very hard to narrow the gap so far. Probably this year, next year, we have to work extremely hard to narrow the gap."; on 2027 balance question: "even we start to spend ... the contribution to this year is almost none, and 2027, a little bit. So we actually, we are looking for 2028-2029 supply, and we hope it's a time that the gap will be narrow. For 2026 and 2027, we are focused on the short-term, more output."; also "their message to me is - silicon from TSMC is a bottleneck".
correction: In January 2026 TSMC did not give 2026-2027 as a balance date. It said it would work to 'narrow the gap' in 2026-2027 through short-term output gains and pointed to 2028-2029, when new fab capacity arrives, as when it hopes the gap narrows. Those remarks were about AI silicon capacity in general, not CoWoS alone.
notes: The 2023-2024 and July 2024 parts check out. The January 2026 remarks are about TSMC's overall AI-silicon capacity (front-end fabs in Taiwan and Arizona), not CoWoS specifically, and the transcript shows expected relief slipping further than the claim says.

original_interpretation: Supply-chain sources (MoneyDJ, via TrendForce, October 2024) expected TSMC CoWoS capacity of 35,000-40,000 wafers per month in 2024, about 80,000 in 2025, and possibly 140,000-150,000 in 2026.
evidence_found: "The report noted that TSMC's CoWoS monthly production capacity is expected to reach 35,000 to 40,000 wafers this year, and surge to 80,000 wafers per month next year." ... "TSMC's CoWoS capacity could still see significant expansion, potentially reaching 140,000 to 150,000 wafers per month by 2026." Article cites "Money DJ, citing supply chain sources" (TrendForce news, 2024-10-21).
notes: Accurately records a dated forecast. The same article notes an earlier expectation of 100,000-120,000 by 2026. A later press estimate (CLM-0797, Dec 2025) put the end-2026 target lower, at 120,000-130,000, so the Oct 2024 top-end forecast has been overtaken. The wafer size in metric.unit is an assumption not stated in the source.

original_interpretation: Taiwanese press (Commercial Times, via TrendForce, December 2025) put TSMC CoWoS capacity at 75,000-80,000 wafers per month in late 2025 with a 2026 target of 120,000-130,000, and reported CoWoS-L and CoWoS-S fully booked.
evidence_found: "Industry estimates cited by the report note that by the end of 2026, TSMC aims to scale monthly CoWoS capacity from today's 75,000–80,000 wafers to as high as 120,000–130,000." (citing Commercial Times); "According to Economic Daily News, a surge of AI and HPC orders from NVIDIA, Google, Amazon, and MediaTek has driven TSMC's entire CoWoS lineup to full capacity, with both CoWoS-L and CoWoS-S fully booked." (TrendForce news, 2025-12-08)
notes: The 2026 figure is an end-of-2026 target (the source says 'by the end of 2026') from industry estimates, not TSMC disclosure. estimate is the right type.

original_interpretation: ASE was reported (December 2025) to be expanding CoWoS-class capacity to 20,000-25,000 wafers per month, more than tripling its output, as OSATs became a second source for TSMC-style advanced packaging.
evidence_found: "Equipment sources cited by Commercial Times project ASE's CoWoS capacity to jump to 20,000–25,000 wafers per month by year-end, more than tripling current output." ... "fueling the rise of a 'TSMC-like' second supply chain centered on OSATs" (TrendForce news, 2025-12-08)
correction: metric.period 'end of 2026' is not supported. The article (8 Dec 2025) says 'by year-end', which most naturally means end-2025, although this is ambiguous. The target date should be recorded as 'by year-end (as of Dec 2025; likely end-2025)'.
notes: The claim text is supported. The source calls it 'CoWoS capacity', and a WebFetch summary wrongly said CoWoP; the raw page text was checked. The problem is metric.period.

original_interpretation: NVIDIA's revenue from customers headquartered in China (including Hong Kong) was US$12.33bn in fiscal 2024, US$25.05bn in fiscal 2025 and US$19.68bn in fiscal 2026, falling from about 19% to about 9% of total revenue.
evidence_found: "Geographic Revenue based upon Customer Headquarters Location (1): (In millions) United States $ 149,617 $ 77,482 $ 31,533 Taiwan (2) 42,345 23,600 14,912 China (including Hong Kong) 19,677 25,048 12,330 Other 4,299 4,367 2,147 Total revenue $ 215,938 $ 130,497 $ 60,922"; "(1) In the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, we changed to revenue based upon the location of our customers' headquarters ... Prior period information has been recast" (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, Notes, segment/geographic information)
notes: Figures match. Shares: FY2025 25,048/130,497 = 19.2% and FY2026 19,677/215,938 = 9.1%. For completeness, FY2024 was 12,330/60,922 = 20.2%, so the '19%' starting point is FY2025, not FY2024. Basis is customer HQ; the 10-K warns that end-customer and shipping location may differ.

original_interpretation: Revenue from US-headquartered customers rose from US$31.5bn (52% of NVIDIA revenue) in fiscal 2024 to US$149.6bn (69%) in fiscal 2026.
evidence_found: "United States $ 149,617 $ 77,482 $ 31,533 ... Total revenue $ 215,938 $ 130,497 $ 60,922" (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, geographic revenue by customer HQ)
notes: 31,533/60,922 = 51.8%, 149,617/215,938 = 69.3%. Customer-HQ basis (recast). Footnote: an estimated 76% of FY2026 Data Center revenue from Taiwan-HQ customers went to end customers in the US and Europe.

original_interpretation: In fiscal 2026 one direct customer accounted for 22% of NVIDIA's total revenue and another for 14%, both mainly in the Compute & Networking segment.
evidence_found: "For fiscal year 2026, sales to one direct customer represented 22% of total revenue and sales to another direct customer represented 14% of total revenue, all of which were primarily attributable to the Compute & Networking segment." (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, Risk Factors and Notes, concentration)
notes: For comparison, FY2025 was 12% plus two at 11%, and FY2024 was one at 13% (same note).

original_interpretation: After US licences granted in August 2025, NVIDIA generated only about US$60 million of H20 revenue in China, and by the FY2026 10-K it had generated no revenue under a February 2026 H200 licence; US officials expected 15% or more of licensed-sale revenue to go to the US government.
evidence_found: "In August 2025, the USG granted licenses that would allow us to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers. We generated approximately $60 million in H20 revenue under those licenses. USG officials expressed an expectation that the USG will receive 15% or more of the revenue generated from licensed sales of our products, but the USG did not publish a regulation codifying such requirement. In February 2026, the USG granted a license that would allow us to ship small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers. To date, we have not generated any revenue under the H200 licensing program" (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, Risk Factors)
notes: As of 10-K filing (early 2026). The same passage adds that H200s shipped under the licence face a 25% US import tariff after a US inspection step.

original_interpretation: NVIDIA's 10-K names TSMC and Samsung as wafer foundries, SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung as memory suppliers, CoWoS as its packaging technology, and Hon Hai, Wistron and Fabrinet as assembly/test contractors.
evidence_found: "We utilize foundries, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited, or TSMC, and Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd., or Samsung, to produce our semiconductor wafers. We purchase memory from SK Hynix Inc., Micron Technology, Inc., and Samsung. We utilize CoWoS technology for semiconductor packaging. We engage with independent subcontractors and contract manufacturers such as Hon Hai Precision Industry Co., Ltd., Wistron Corporation, and Fabrinet to perform assembly, testing and packaging of our final products." (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, Item 1 Business, Manufacturing)

original_interpretation: NVIDIA lists large cloud companies with internal chip teams (Alibaba, Alphabet, Amazon, Baidu, Huawei, Microsoft) among its competitors, alongside AMD, Huawei and Intel.
evidence_found: "Our current competitors include: • suppliers and licensors of hardware and software for discrete and integrated GPUs, custom chips and other accelerated computing solutions ... such as Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., or AMD, Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd., or Huawei, and Intel Corporation, or Intel; • large cloud services companies with internal teams designing hardware and software ... such as Alibaba Group, Alphabet Inc., Amazon, Inc., or Amazon, Baidu, Inc., Huawei, and Microsoft Corporation, or Microsoft" (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, Item 1 Business, Competition)

original_interpretation: In fiscal 2026 NVIDIA introduced NVLink Fusion so hyperscalers and custom ASIC designers can connect their own CPUs and XPUs to NVIDIA's platform.
evidence_found: "In fiscal year 2026, we introduced NVIDIA NVLink Fusion to enable hyperscalers and custom ASIC designers to integrate custom CPUs and XPUs with our platform." (NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, Item 1 Business)
notes: The company's description of its own product, so reported_claim is correct even though it comes from a filing.

original_interpretation: Amazon's CEO said in October 2025 that Trainium2 was fully subscribed, had become a multibillion-dollar business growing 150% quarter on quarter, and that Project Rainier for Anthropic was heading to about 1 million Trainium2 chips by end-2025.
evidence_found: Jassy (prepared remarks): "...containing nearly 500,000 of our Trainium2 chips. Anthropic is using it now to build and deploy its industry-leading AI model, Claude, which we expect to be on more than 1 million Trainium2 chips by year-end. Trainium2 continues to see strong adoption, is fully subscribed is now a multibillion-dollar business that grew 150% quarter-over-quarter."; Q&A: "it's not simple to be able to build a cluster that has 500,000 plus chips going to 1 million." (Motley Fool transcript, Amazon Q3 2025 call)
correction: Project Rainier had nearly 500,000 Trainium2 chips. The 'more than 1 million Trainium2 chips by year-end' is what Amazon expected Claude/Anthropic to run on in total, not necessarily Rainier alone, and the figure is 'more than', not 'about', 1 million.
notes: The Trainium2 statements are verified verbatim. Motley Fool is a secondary transcript host (financial_press, tier 2), which is honest.

original_interpretation: Amazon's CEO said AWS added more than 3.8 GW of power in the 12 months to Q3 2025, expected to double capacity again by 2027, and that across the industry 'maybe the bottleneck is power'.
evidence_found: "adding more than 3.8 gigawatts of power in the past 12 months, more than any other cloud provider. To put that into perspective, we're now double the power capacity that AWS was in 2022, and we're on track to double again by 2027."; Q&A: "we expect to double our overall capacity by the end of 2027. So we're bringing in quite a bit of capacity today, overall in the industry, maybe the bottleneck is power. I think at some point, it may move to chips" (Motley Fool transcript, Amazon Q3 2025 call)
notes: Jassy immediately qualifies the remark: the bottleneck 'may move to chips'.

original_interpretation: Anthropic announced in October 2025 it would expand its use of Google Cloud to up to one million TPUs, worth tens of billions of dollars and bringing well over a gigawatt of capacity online in 2026, while also using AWS Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs.
evidence_found: "we plan to expand our use of Google Cloud technologies, including up to one million TPUs"; "The expansion is worth tens of billions of dollars and is expected to bring well over a gigawatt of capacity online in 2026."; "Anthropic's unique compute strategy focuses on a diversified approach that efficiently uses three chip platforms–Google's TPUs, Amazon's Trainium, and NVIDIA's GPUs." (Anthropic news, 23 Oct 2025)
notes: A company announcement, correctly typed as reported_claim / company_documentation.

original_interpretation: TrendForce forecast (January 2026) that global AI server shipments would grow more than 28% in 2026, with GPU-based servers at 69.7% of shipments and ASIC-based servers at about 27.8%, their highest share since 2023.
evidence_found: "AI server shipments are expected to surge by more than 28% YoY"; "GPUs will remain the leading category, accounting for 69.7% of shipments"; "The share of ASIC-based AI servers is expected to reach 27.8% by 2026, the highest since 2023" (TrendForce press release, 20 Jan 2026)
notes: Shares are of unit shipments. This is a forecast and correctly typed as an estimate.

original_interpretation: By revenue, merchant GPUs still dwarfed custom accelerators through 2025: NVIDIA's fiscal-2026 Data Center revenue (US$193.7bn) was nearly ten times Broadcom's fiscal-2025 AI revenue (about US$20bn, which also includes networking), although ASIC servers were forecast at about 28% of AI server units in 2026.
evidence_found: Inputs re-checked: NVIDIA FY2026 10-K end-market table "Data Center $ 193,737 ... Compute 162,361 ... Networking 31,376" (SRC-0079); Broadcom FY2025 AI revenue about US$20bn (CLM-0759, verified medium); TrendForce ASIC share 27.8% of 2026 AI server units (SRC-0266). 193.7/20 = 9.7.
correction: Restate as: 'NVIDIA's FY2026 Data Center revenue (US$193.7bn, incl. US$31.4bn networking) was about 9.7x Broadcom's FY2025 AI revenue (~US$20bn, incl. networking); Broadcom is the largest but not the only custom-accelerator vendor, so this indicates but does not measure the merchant-vs-custom split.'
notes: The arithmetic is right and the input claims are verified. The inference over-reaches, though. Broadcom's AI revenue is not the whole custom-accelerator market: it excludes Marvell, Alchip, GUC, MediaTek and hyperscaler in-house spend, and it includes Ethernet networking. NVIDIA Data Center includes US$31.4bn of networking plus systems and software. A compute-to-compute comparison would be US$162.4bn against an undisclosed XPU-only share of Broadcom's ~US$20bn.

original_interpretation: TrendForce reported in July 2025 that the supply gap for low-CTE (T-glass) fiberglass used in IC substrates had widened to over 10%, with new Nitto Boseki (Nittobo) T-glass capacity not expected until the second half of 2026.
evidence_found: "On the materials front, a structural shortage is hitting high-grade fiberglass fabrics. Commercial Times notes that Japanese suppliers have shifted production toward high-margin specialty materials like low-Dk and low-CTE fiberglass, widening the supply gap to over 10%." ... "Commercial Times notes that with new T-Glass capacity from Nitto Boseki not expected until the second half of 2026, the short-term supply crunch is unlikely to ease" (TrendForce news, 2025-07-22, citing Commercial Times)
correction: The 'over 10%' supply gap is attributed to Commercial Times (relayed by TrendForce), not TrendForce research. It refers to high-grade fiberglass fabrics in general, as Japanese suppliers shift to low-Dk and low-CTE grades, not specifically to low-CTE T-glass.
notes: TrendForce is relaying a Commercial Times report, not publishing its own TrendForce analysis. Nitto Boseki timing is verified.

original_interpretation: Taiwanese IC substrate makers raised prices from July 2025, by up to 20% for T-glass-based BT substrates, while ABF substrate shipments surged on AI chip and HBM packaging demand.
evidence_found: "Taiwanese IC substrate makers have been raising prices since July, especially for T-Glass-based BT (Bismaleimide Triazine) products — with increases up to 20% in some cases." ... "Beyond BT substrates, ABF (Ajinomoto Build-up Film) shipments are surging as well, driven by rising AI chip demand and the shift toward multi-chip and HBM packaging." (TrendForce news, 2025-07-22, citing Commercial Times supply-chain sources)
notes: Press report via Commercial Times. The claim_type 'estimate' is loose, since these are reported market developments rather than a modelled figure, and reported_claim would fit better. Either way, confidence stays tier-2.

original_interpretation: The IEA estimated data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024 (about 1.5% of world consumption) and projected this to more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030.
evidence_found: "Data centres accounted for around 1.5% of the world's electricity consumption in 2024, or 415 terawatt-hours (TWh)."; "Data centre electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030" (IEA, Energy and AI, Executive Summary, 2025, Base Case). Newer: "Our updated projections see electricity consumption from data centres roughly doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, accounting for around 3% of global electricity demand by that date."; "The global electricity demand of data centres ... grew by 17% in 2025, in line with IEA projections." (IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI, Executive Summary, 2026)
correction: IEA's 2026 update (Key Questions on Energy and AI) estimates data-centre electricity use at 485 TWh in 2025 (+17%) and projects about 950 TWh by 2030 (~3% of global demand), superseding the 945 TWh 2030 projection. New claim added (supersedes CLM-0815).
notes: The 2024 figure is still consistent (485/1.17 ≈ 415 TWh). The 2030 projection has been updated and a 2025 actual estimate is now available.

original_interpretation: The IEA warned that around 20% of planned data-centre projects could be delayed unless grid risks are addressed.
evidence_found: "Unless these risks are addressed, around 20% of planned data centre projects could be at risk of delays." (IEA, Energy and AI, Executive Summary, 2025)
notes: A 2025 IEA assessment. The 2026 update (Key Questions on Energy and AI) speaks qualitatively of bottlenecks 'reducing the likelihood of more aggressive near-term scenarios' and does not restate a percentage. estimate is the right type.

original_interpretation: Measured by the whole WSTS market, the AI wave's growth so far is similar in pace to the mid-1990s PC boom but far larger in dollars: the market grew 51% from 2023 to 2025 (US$526.9bn to US$795.6bn, +US$269bn), versus 141% over 1992-1995 (US$59.9bn to US$144.4bn, +US$84bn) and 37% in the single year 2000.
correction: By these figures the AI wave has been slower in percentage terms than the mid-1990s PC boom: about 23% a year compounded (51% over 2023-2025) against about 34% a year (141% over 1992-1995). It is much larger in dollars: +US$269bn against +US$84bn.
notes: The numbers are right. The phrase 'similar in pace' is not supported. Also, the 2025 figure (CLM-0030, WSTS press release, unverified) comes from a different vintage than the Blue Book series used for the other years.

original_interpretation: Unlike the PC and smartphone waves, which lifted broad product categories, the AI wave's gains are concentrated in a few firms: NVIDIA's annual Data Center revenue alone rose by about US$179bn between fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2026, comparable to the whole WSTS market's US$269bn increase over 2023-2025.
evidence_found: Recomputed: NVIDIA Data Center FY2023 US$15.01bn (CLM-0741) to FY2026 US$193.7bn (CLM-0744; 10-K table "Data Center $ 193,737 $ 115,186 $ 47,525") = +US$178.7bn. WSTS 2023 to 2025 = +US$268.7bn (CLM-0630, CLM-0030). FY2024 to FY2026 = 193.7 - 47.5 = +US$146.2bn.
correction: The comparison uses mismatched spans. NVIDIA FY2023 to FY2026 is roughly CY2022-CY2025 (three years), while the WSTS increase covers 2023-2025 (two years). The like-for-like NVIDIA increase (FY2024 to FY2026, about CY2023-CY2025) is about US$146bn, not US$179bn.
notes: The claim is an interpretation. The concentration point is plausible and consistent with Omdia's CLM-0721, which is itself unverified. The contrast with the PC and smartphone waves ('lifted broad product categories') has no cited evidence. NVIDIA Data Center revenue also includes systems and networking, not only chips counted by WSTS.
